rewrites.summary:
Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009 — organisers mark seventeen consecutive years 'without fail', run 'as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics', the 2025 edition under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro. Organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as confirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

The festival draws a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation: in September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches from Banwoldang station along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans, timed against the festival. For a visible trans visitor the result is a concentrated confrontational environment during festival week; the event itself continues to take place annually despite interference.

An annual, well-organised counter-mobilisation by a regional conservative-religious umbrella accompanies the festival — its most recent edition gathered roughly 3,500 participants from about 1,600 churches along a 450-metre route timed against the event. rewrites.summary:
In October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo, holding the military should have considered her a woman when reviewing fitness for duty — a ruling widely described as a landmark in the case brought to repeal the discharge decision.

On 24 June 2024, after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's original 'natural death' classification and recognised the 2021 death as service-related, Byun was interred at the National Cemetery in Daejeon. Around 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, arguing her service did not qualify her for interment there: state recognition of a trans person at the national memorial ground, met with a small but public rejection in open space.

In June 2024, after the defence ministry reclassified the soldier's 2021 death as service-related, she was buried at the national cemetery located here; roughly 60 activists protested the interment — a small, visible public rejection accompanying a state act of recognition.

rewrites.summary:
The model student human-rights ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province; Seoul's office adopted it in 2012 and it spread to other regional offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave.

When Seoul's metropolitan council — pushed by a campaign begun by religious and parents' coalitions in August 2022 — abolished the capital's ordinance on 26 April 2024, Gyeonggi stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher warned that wholesale abolition 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector'. The province's standing is thus origin-and-retention of student protections rather than any enforcement measure aimed at visitors.

When the capital's council abolished its version in April 2024 after a religious-coalition campaign, this province was among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances. The record is about student protections and institutional posture, not visitor-facing measures.

rewrites.summary:
Since 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German has been prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration in Bavaria, implementing the Söder government declaration of December 2023 through a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities. Coverage notes critics dismissing the measure as symbol politics while recording its practical reach across every public counter, registry office and classroom a visitor might deal with.

Bavaria is also a partner — with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt — in a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) on legal gender change: an organised state-level attempt to make the nationwide self-ID law stricter, which critics see as restricting how trans and intersex people use the right.

The state is a partner in an upper-house initiative, with three other Länder, to tighten the federal self-determination law on legal gender change — an organised sub-national attempt to restrict the existing right rather than an enacted change.

rewrites.summary:
Germany's Pride movement faces a documented rise in attacks: the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-motivated attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including a boiling-water attack, and runs a €100,000 support fund weighted to eastern Germany. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day, with hundreds of thousands expected, Berlin's organisers nonetheless urged participants to 'be vigilant'.

The reporting also situates the capital: Maneo, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades like Berlin's had not been specifically threatened — smaller towns are hardest to police — while everyday hostility still surfaces: one Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in eighteen months.

Local anti-violence documentation, however, notes big-city parades here were not specifically threatened (smaller towns are hardest to police), while routine homophobic incidents persist: one neighbourhood venue alone logged 45 police complaints over eighteen months.

rewrites.summary:
In Cottbus on 20 October 2025, a rubbish container was set alight against the façade of the 'Regenbogenkombinat' queer cultural centre during CSD week; the fire was out in about fifteen minutes and nobody was hurt, but state security (Staatsschutz) took over the arson investigation and a political motive cannot be excluded — local initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the attack sits among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city.

The subsequent Cottbus CSD — the 17th edition, under the motto 'Vereint in Frieden und Vielfalt' — ran with a large police presence against two registered far-right counter-demonstrations, one organised by 'Deutsche Jugend voran', and proceeded without major disruption. The local queer community describes itself as unusually watchful: repeated physical pressure on infrastructure, met by a functioning protective response.

rewrites.summary:
A Hessen Landtag small inquiry with the Interior Minister's answer (April 2025) records police-registered queer-hostile offences rising from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024 — a year-on-year jump of 52 that the minister's reply calls alarming.

The trend must be read with the federal BKA's own caveat: its situation report on LSBTIQ* security introduced a new reporting category that makes state-by-state comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so rises may partly reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger. The same answer notes the 2010-established network of LSBTIQ* liaison officers in every police headquarters, governed by a standing framework concept — an institutional response in place while the statistics remain ambiguous.

rewrites.summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three Länder — with Sachsen and Thüringen — that brought a Bundesrat initiative (reported June 2026) to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act on legal gender change, proposing an 'abuse review' mechanism with objective, documentable grounds for registry-office intervention. The trigger cited is the 'Fall Liebich' — a convicted far-right extremist whose legal gender was changed after sentencing.

The initiative is an attempt, not a change: it is backed by Union MPs, resisted by the SPD, and runs against a scheduled federal evaluation of the SBGG that the family ministry is conducting and whose SPD-led ministries consider the existing law sufficient. No standing administrative ban or documented street-attack pattern specific to this state was identified in the research pass.

The tightening remains a proposal: resisted by the junior federal partner and set against a scheduled government evaluation of the current law. No equivalent standing administrative ban was documented here.

rewrites.summary:
Wales's devolved administration has publicly maintained its LGBTQ+ Action Plan through the UK's post-judgment years: the plan's standing update page was issued answering the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, with a dedicated young-people's edition posted January 2026.

Its 'Rights, Respect, Equality' statutory school guidance (consultation May 2025) obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on the grounds of sex, gender reassignment and sexual orientation, with incident recording and monitoring and a parental escalation route. The practical facility rules set state-wide are unchanged here, but the visible institutional commitment — maintained action plan, statutory recording duties — is an official posture of inclusion at a national moment of rollback.

rewrites.summary:
Victoria's Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025, created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, plus personal association; the civil grounds commenced 15 April 2026. The state human-rights commission's explainer records public incitement against a trans person becoming criminally chargeable alongside civil recourse.

A coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women in Melbourne during the pandemic — lead case Bridget Flack, missing December 2020 — found Victoria Police failed the search, and Coroner Ingrid Giles made nine recommendations including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons risk practice; the government is reviewing them. The inquest documents a serious institutional failure; the 2025 legislation and the review process are the corrective response.
